extraction.name: Vibravox
extraction.description: Vibravox is a dataset compliant with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) containing audio recordings using five different body-conduction audio sensors: two in-ear microphones, two bone conduction vibration pickups, and a laryngophone. The dataset also includes audio data from an airborne microphone used as a reference. The Vibravox corpus contains 45 hours per sensor of speech samples and physiological sounds recorded by 188 participants under different acoustic conditions imposed by a high order ambisonics 3D spatializer.
extraction.creator: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poirée, Véronique Zimpfer, and Éric Bavu
extraction.citeAs: J. Hauret, M. Olivier, C. Langrenne, S. Poirée, and É. Bavu, 'vibravox (revision 071945b),' 2024. [Online]. Available: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Cnam-LMSSC/vibravox
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The recording process consists of four steps performed consecutively for each participant: speech-clean (reading sentences sourced from the French Wikipedia for 15 minutes), speechless-noisy (remaining silent in a noisy environment for 2 minutes and 24 seconds), speechless-clean (remaining silent in complete silence for 54 seconds), and speech-noisy (reading sentences in a noisy environment for 54 seconds).
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: A small number of audio clips had various shortcomings: Mispronounced sentences, sensors shifting from their initial positions, occasional sensor malfunctions, or instances where a microphone was inadvertently left unequipped led to some data inconsistencies.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Audio recordings using five different body-conduction audio sensors (two in-ear microphones, two bone conduction vibration pickups, and a laryngophone) and an airborne microphone. The text utilized for participant readings originates from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice. Ambient noise samples were sourced from Audio Set and in-house recordings of concerts and street events.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Applied textual filters that excluded most proper names, retaining only common first names, French town or region names, and country names. Utterances containing numbers, Greek letters, mathematical symbols, or syntactic errors were carefully removed. Applied common text normalization operations, such as lowercasing text and removing punctuation except for apostrophes.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A 20 Hz high-pass filter is uniformly applied to each acquisition channel. A series of three automatic filters were applied to remove utterances with obvious deficiencies: 1) Discard audio samples where Phoneme Error Rate (PER) > 10%. 2) Verify sensor functioning by checking SNR > 1.5 dB. 3) Detect potential sensitivity drift by checking that speech energy is greater than silence energy. Timestamps generated by Voice Activity Detection were extended by 0.6 seconds on both sides.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Generated the corresponding phonetic transcription using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA), which contains 33 phonemes in French, using the text phonemizer of the CoML lab. A phase of manual phonetic transcription was then necessary for unrecognized words to preserve the minimal French phonetic alphabet.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: text phonemizer of the CoML lab
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For some words, the phonemizer produced some language switches that we wanted to avoid, to preserve the minimal French phonetic alphabet. A phase of manual phonetic transcription was then necessary for these unrecognized words.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: text phonemizer of the CoML lab, whisper-timestamped model
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Gender, age, and biometric information (everyone's skull and timbre are unique, heart rate, breathing).
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Proficiency in this realm with BCMs can confer significant advantages, particularly in military operations or industrial settings. Robust speaker identification systems are essential in contexts where heavy machinery is operated via voice commands, ensuring rigorous safety protocols are upheld.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The temple sensor exhibits the smallest bandwidth, barely recording any speech signal above 1500 Hz. The soft and rigid in-ear sensors exhibit larger bandwidths yet display clear antiresonance frequencies. The forehead accelerometer offers the largest bandwidth but does not effectively filter out external noise pollution. In some cases, such as when a participant's ear canal was too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing, post-processing filters were not triggered.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation for bandwidth extension (speech enhancement), speech-to-phonemes recognition (ASR), and speaker verification. Developing voice commands and monitoring vital signs, including heart rate.
